summary: The verb is to draw someone out, and each of its three uses is out of water: Pharaoh’s daughter draws the child from the Nile and names him מֹשֶׁה for it (Exo 2:10), and David says Yahweh “drew me out of many waters”, set beside “he took me” and “he delivered me from my strong enemy” (2Sa 22:17–18; Psa 18:17–18). The name Moses is the root’s chief word in scripture, about 770 times; its own entry is under names. Jewish Aramaic has the same verb for handling, wiping with the hand and drawing a thing through water.

words.summary: Three uses only, all of drawing a person out of water to save his life; scripture’s own explanation of the name Moses rests on it. So few uses fix little beyond that.

senses.definition: Lift a person out of water by hand: Pharaoh’s daughter takes the child out of the river into which Pharaoh had ordered every son cast.

evidence.note: וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ מֹשֶׁה וַתֹּאמֶר כִּי מִן־הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ, “she called his name Moses and said, For out of the water I drew him.”
She sends her maid, takes the ark from among the reeds of the river: what “drew him out” describes.
Pharaoh’s order: every son born you shall cast into the river.
Stephen retells the verse: when he was set out, Pharaoh’s daughter ἀνείλετο αὐτόν, took him up, and brought him up as her own son.

senses.gloss: draw out of many waters, rescue
senses.definition: Of Yahweh, to reach down and pull the sufferer out of overwhelming waters; the next line says what the waters are: a strong enemy and those who hate him.

evidence.note: יִשְׁלַח מִמָּרוֹם יִקָּחֵנִי יַמְשֵׁנִי מִמַּיִם רַבִּים, “he sent from on high, he took me, he drew me out of many waters.”
יַצִּילֵנִי מֵאֹיְבִי עָז, “he delivered me from my strong enemy and from those who hated me”: the many waters are the enemy.
The same words in the song as 2 Samuel keeps it.
“He brought me out into a broad place”: the end of the rescue.
Stephen uses the Septuagint’s word for Exo 2:10: Pharaoh’s daughter ἀνείλετο αὐτόν.

parallels.note: “He took me” is the line’s first verb, “he drew me out” its second.
The next line: “he delivered me (יַצִּילֵנִי) from my strong enemy”.

phrases.gloss: out of the water I drew him
he drew me out of many waters

cognates.gloss: feel, touch; rub, wash (the hands); aphel handle, draw (through water)
cognates.note: The Targums and Talmud use the verb for working with the hand: feeling (Targ. Onkelos Gen 27:22), wiping and washing the hands, and in the aphel drawing a man’s clothes through water (B. Bathra 153a). The aphel answers closely to the Hebrew, a causative of drawing something by hand through or out of water. Aramaic š, not t, behind ש.

A verb of the hand, like the Aramaic; Arabic s answers to Hebrew ש from š, as the Aramaic does. Not found in the vendored Lane, whose article مسى (p. 3020) gives only the root’s “evening” words; so it rests on Wiktionary alone and is left possible.

evidence.locator: Arabic مسى (masā), verb, root م س ي

doctrine.statement: Pharaoh ordered every Hebrew son cast into the river (Exo 1:22); the child was laid among the reeds of that river and drawn out of it, and named for being drawn out (Exo 2:3–10). David uses the same verb of Yahweh’s rescue of him, and says what the “many waters” were: a strong enemy and those who hated him (Psa 18:17–18). Isaiah recalls Moses in the same terms turned outward: Yahweh “who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock … dividing the water before them” (Isa 63:11–12), the day Yahweh saved Israel and Israel saw Egypt dead on the shore of the sea (Exo 14:30); Stephen calls the man God sent “ruler and deliverer” the one Israel had refused (Act 7:35), and Paul says the fathers “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1Co 10:1–2). From the verses: the one who was drawn out of the water of death was the one through whom Yahweh drew his people out of the sea, and a deliverance out of water is scripture’s own figure for being saved from death by God’s hand.

note: Drafted 2026-11-13. The root’s only scripture words are the verb (m.ds.aa) and the name Moses (m.ds.ab, and xm.am.ab for the Aramaic of Ezr 6:18; the database counts the same tokens under both), which is in names/mosheh.json. The name has the shape of the qal active participle (as רֹעֶה, עֹשֶׂה), “one drawing out”, not the passive “one drawn out”; Exo 2:10 explains it from the verb without saying which; Isa 63:11 (מֹשֶׁה עַמּוֹ … הַמַּעֲלֵם מִיָּם) may play on it. Not this root: נִמְשִׁי Nimshi (BDB files it n.dr.af under נמר); מַשֶּׁה “loan” of Deu 15:2 (m.ds.ac, under נשׁה). Leads not followed: Arabic masā “put the hand into a she-camel’s womb and draw out the foetus” (not in the vendored Lane; Lane’s supplement or Taj al-ʿArus would be the place); Syriac ܡܫܐ “wipe, cleanse” (not in SEDRA; Payne Smith not checked); Akkadian mašāʾu “take away by force” (Oracc; third radical ʾ, not y, and the sense is far, so not recorded); Jastrow compares מוּשׁ/מָשַׁשׁ “feel”, which may be a related root (Targ. Onkelos uses מְשֵׁי for Hebrew מוּשׁ in Gen 27:22). The Peshitta New Testament has no word of this root in SEDRA. Egyptian msi̯ “give birth; fashion” (TLA tla74950, Wb 2, 137.4–138.17) and ms “child” (tla74750), as in Ḏḥw.tj-ms.w Tuthmosis (tla400441) and the personal names Ms (tla600129) and Ms.w (tla702426), are proposed as the source of the name; not recorded as a cognate, since the validator allows Egyptian only as a loan and the evidence is against one: scripture explains the name from the Hebrew verb (Exo 2:10), and where it writes Egyptian -ms- it writes ס, not ש (רַעְמְסֵס, Gen 47:11; Exo 1:11; 12:37).
